title: How Evals and Prompts Shape Agent Behavior — Preetika Bhateja & Daniel Bump, YouTube Ads

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: The agent's application domain is YouTube advertising—transforming messy advertising creatives (low-quality images, cluttered visuals, heavy text overlays) into clean, reusable assets for downstream generative AI tools. This is a creative-production system in the media and advertising vertical.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The evaluation methodology lessons—vibing, golden sets, scale raters, LLM-as-judge, trace inspection, pattern-based evaluation, launch gatekeeping—are broadly applicable across all agent development domains, not specific to advertising.

summary: The YouTube Ads team at Google shares practical lessons from building evaluation workflows for an LLM-based agent that transforms messy advertising creatives into clean, reusable assets. Speakers Preetika Bhateja (Product Manager), Daniel Bump (Engineer), and Chris Souza present at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. They argue agent reliability depends on three pillars: capabilities, guardrails, and evals, all developed together. Before agent-level evals, they recommend optimizing LLM-friendly tools and adding an independent critique agent with remediation loops. They describe an evolutionary evaluation approach: starting with 'vibing'—intuition-based, non-scalable manual inspection that enables radical architectural changes—then scaling to human raters with clear rubrics and explanations beyond pass/fail, and finally LLM-as-judge with agreement-rate monitoring and spot checks on reasoning. A key demonstration shows a disclaimer-removal bug where the agent acknowledged a guardrail in its trace yet still violated it—a failure only visible through trace inspection, not categorical pass rates. They emphasize pattern-based evaluation over isolated runs due to non-determinism, hill climbing through iterative eval-agent co-development with precision/recall and ablations, understanding regressions to distinguish acceptable trade-offs from critical failures, refreshing test sets with production data, investing in online evals, and defining clear launch gatekeeping criteria early.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts form a unified evaluation lifecycle for production LLM agents. The evolutionary path from vibing to scaled raters to LLM-as-judge mirrors the SE progression from manual debugging to systematic testing to automated CI/CD. Trace inspection bridges both domains—it is simultaneously a debugging technique (SE) and a method for understanding agent reasoning (AI). Golden sets, ablation experiments, and regression analysis are SE testing methodologies adapted for the unique challenge of non-deterministic AI systems, where traditional single-run pass/fail is insufficient. The critique agent with remediation loops is an AI-native pattern serving the SE goal of self-correcting systems. Launch gatekeeping criteria apply traditional release management discipline to AI deployment, while multi-output evaluation acknowledges that AI quality is multi-dimensional rather than binary. Together, these concepts address the central tension: how to build reliable systems from non-deterministic components, using progressively more rigorous evaluation as the system matures from prototype to production.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 on July 1, 2026 (Day 3, Evals track) at Moscone West, San Francisco. The video was published on YouTube on July 24-25, 2026. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026. The talk reflects the state of LLM agent evaluation practices at Google/YouTube in mid-2026, a period when LLM-as-judge and agent observability tooling were rapidly maturing in the industry.
takeaways: Agent reliability is a function of capabilities, guardrails, and evals—all three must be developed together
Optimize individual LLM-friendly tools and add a critique agent with remediation loop before attempting agent-level evals
Early 'vibing' (intuition-based iteration) is valuable before formal evals—it enables radical changes and deep failure understanding
Start small with core tasks and negative tests, then expand the golden set gradually
Collect rater explanations, not just pass/fail—critical for multi-output cases and targeting agent improvements
Examine agent trace logs to diagnose failures invisible to categorical pass-rate metrics
Focus on failure patterns across multiple golden-set examples rather than hyperfixating on isolated runs, due to non-determinism
Understand regressions to distinguish acceptable trade-offs from critical failures during launch readiness
Define clear launch gatekeeping criteria early—precision/recall thresholds or other metrics appropriate to the eval type
Keep evals evolving: refresh test sets with production data, invest in online evals, and update golden sets as use cases mature

concepts.name: LLM-as-Judge
concepts.explanation: Using LLMs as automated evaluators that score or assess agent outputs, calibrated against human raters by monitoring agreement/disagreement rates and conducting spot checks on the LLM's reasoning.
concepts.importance: LLM-as-judge enables scalable evaluation that would be infeasible with human raters alone, but only if properly calibrated—monitoring agreement rates ensures the judge remains trustworthy.

concepts.name: Critique Agent with Remediation Loop
concepts.explanation: An independent agent that reviews another agent's output and attempts self-correction before final delivery. The speakers recommend adding this as a foundational agent architecture pattern before attempting agent-level evals.
concepts.importance: The critique agent is a self-correction mechanism that catches errors at generation time, reducing the burden on downstream evaluation and improving overall reliability.

concepts.name: Agent Guardrails
concepts.explanation: Rules and constraints designed to prevent agents from taking unwanted actions. The disclaimer-removal bug demonstrates that guardrails can fail when the agent acknowledges a rule yet still violates it in edge cases.
concepts.importance: Guardrails are a primary reliability mechanism, but the talk shows they are insufficient alone—they must be paired with evals that test negative cases and trace inspection to detect violations.

concepts.name: Vibing (Intuition-Based Evaluation)
concepts.explanation: An early-stage, non-scalable approach where developers manually inspect agent outputs, make radical architectural changes, and develop deep understanding of failure patterns before formalizing evaluation.
concepts.importance: Vibing enables rapid iteration and deep domain understanding before the overhead of formal evals is justified, though it does not scale and must eventually transition to structured evaluation.

concepts.name: Multi-Output Evaluation
concepts.explanation: Evaluating agent outputs across multiple dimensions simultaneously—such as accuracy, brand safety, and expected behavior—requiring nuanced rubrics and rater explanations rather than simple pass/fail.
concepts.importance: Real-world agent tasks rarely have a single correct output; multi-output evaluation captures the full complexity of agent quality and identifies which specific dimensions need improvement.

concepts.name: Non-Determinism in Generative AI
concepts.explanation: LLM outputs are non-deterministic—an agent may succeed on one attempt and fail on another with the same input. This property necessitates pattern-based evaluation across multiple runs rather than fixating on isolated examples.
concepts.importance: Non-determinism fundamentally changes evaluation methodology: single-run pass/fail is unreliable, requiring multiple examples per pattern and aggregate failure analysis to draw valid conclusions.

concepts.name: Hill Climbing via Eval-Agent Co-Development
concepts.explanation: Iterative quality improvement achieved by co-developing evaluation sets and agent capabilities in tandem—reviewing eval results, computing precision and recall, adjusting models and tooling, and re-evaluating.
concepts.importance: This co-development approach ensures evals and agents evolve together, preventing the common failure mode of building evals after the agent is 'done' and discovering systemic issues too late.

concepts.name: LLM-Friendly Tools
concepts.explanation: Tools designed specifically for LLM consumption that are optimized before attempting agent-level evaluation. The speakers recommend this as a prerequisite to agent-level evals.
concepts.importance: Tool quality is a prerequisite for agent quality—optimizing LLM-friendly tools first isolates tool-level issues from agent-level reasoning issues, making subsequent agent evals more meaningful.

concepts.name: Golden Set Construction
concepts.explanation: A curated collection of test cases (positive and negative) used to evaluate agent behavior, with multiple examples per failure pattern to account for non-deterministic outputs. The speakers recommend starting small with core tasks and negative tests, then expanding gradually.
concepts.importance: Golden sets are the foundational test artifact for agent evaluation—they provide the ground truth against which agent quality is measured and regression is detected.

concepts.name: Trace Inspection and Log Debugging
concepts.explanation: Examining agent execution traces/logs to diagnose failures that are invisible to categorical pass-rate metrics. The speakers demonstrate this with a disclaimer-removal bug where the agent explicitly acknowledged a rule in its trace yet still violated it.
concepts.importance: Trace inspection is the primary debugging technique for understanding why an agent failed, revealing failure modes that aggregate metrics cannot surface.

concepts.name: Ablation Experiments
concepts.explanation: Controlled experiments that isolate individual changes (prompt modifications, tool updates, model versions) to measure their impact on agent quality. The speakers describe running ablations alongside eval-agent co-development to climb the quality ladder.
concepts.importance: Ablations provide causal evidence for which changes improve or degrade agent performance, enabling data-driven iteration rather than guesswork.

concepts.name: Regression Analysis
concepts.explanation: Analyzing regressions in agent behavior to distinguish acceptable trade-offs from critical failures during launch readiness. The speakers warn against hyperfixating on isolated examples and instead advocate examining failure patterns across multiple golden-set runs.
concepts.importance: Regression analysis directly informs launch decisions—knowing whether a regression is an acceptable trade-off or a critical failure determines whether an agent is production-ready.

concepts.name: Inter-Rater Reliability
concepts.explanation: Establishing strong human-human agreement on evaluation rubrics within the team before scaling to external raters. The speakers emphasize clear rubrics with examples and collecting explanations rather than just pass/fail verdicts.
concepts.importance: Without strong inter-rater reliability, evaluation results are noisy and unreliable, making it impossible to distinguish genuine agent improvements from rating variance.

concepts.name: Online Evaluation and Production Monitoring
concepts.explanation: Continuously evaluating agent behavior in production using real-world data to detect drift and ensure ongoing quality. The speakers stress investing in online evals and keeping data representative of real-world usage.
concepts.importance: Online evals close the loop between development-time testing and production reality, catching issues that only emerge at scale with diverse, real inputs.

concepts.name: Launch Readiness and Gatekeeping Criteria
concepts.explanation: Defining clear metrics and thresholds (e.g., precision/recall targets) that must be met before deploying an agent to production. The speakers advocate establishing these criteria early in development.
concepts.importance: Gatekeeping criteria provide objective, pre-committed decision rules for production release, preventing subjective or pressure-driven launches of insufficiently evaluated agents.

concepts.name: Test Set Maintenance and Refresh
concepts.explanation: Periodically updating evaluation test sets with production data to ensure they remain representative of real-world use cases as they evolve over time.
concepts.importance: Stale test sets lead to false confidence—an agent may pass outdated tests while failing on current production patterns, making refresh essential for sustained reliability.

sections.title: Introduction and Agent Building Challenges
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves as part of the YouTube ads team working on image and video models. They frame the difficulty of building reliable agents and position evals as a key tool for managing non-deterministic agent behavior in production.

sections.title: Agent Foundation: Tools, Critique Agent, and Evals
sections.summary: Recommends starting with a focused, strong set of LLM-friendly tools optimized before agent-level evals. Suggests adding an independent critique agent with remediation loop for self-correction. Emphasizes that strong evals are essential for proving the value of changes and running ablation experiments to climb the quality ladder.

sections.title: Reliability, Vibing, and Starting Small
sections.summary: Defines reliability as a function of capabilities, guardrails, and evals. Advocates for early 'vibing'—an intuition-based, non-scalable approach that allows rapid iteration, radical architecture changes, and deep understanding of failure patterns. Warns against jumping to scaled raters too early. Recommends starting small with core tasks and testing negatives before expanding the golden set.

sections.title: Working with Scale Raters
sections.summary: Shares lessons for involving cross-functional scale raters: provide clear rubrics with examples, ensure strong human-human agreement within the team, and collect explanations rather than just pass/fail. Highlights that multi-output cases (accuracy, brand safety, expected behavior) require nuanced rating and explanations to identify specific agent weaknesses.

sections.title: LLM-as-Judge and Agreement Monitoring
sections.summary: Describes using LLM/auto raters: monitor agreement/disagreement rates between human and LLM raters to track trends, go beyond pass/fail by examining agent traces, conduct spot checks on LLM reasoning, and maintain high-quality ground truth with broad use-case coverage and strong human-human agreement.

sections.title: Agent Trace Example and Generalization Limits
sections.summary: Demonstrates the value of trace inspection with a disclaimer-removal bug: despite explicit instructions, the agent detected a disclaimer and then removed it anyway. Categorical pass rates could not surface this failure. Concludes that agents, like all ML systems, do not generalize well depending on training data distributions.

sections.title: Hill Climbing, Launch Readiness, and Pattern-Based Evaluation
sections.summary: Discusses iterative hill climbing through co-developing evals and agents—reviewing eval sets, computing precision and recall, and adjusting models, tooling, and rating guides. Emphasizes understanding regressions to distinguish acceptable trade-offs from critical failures. Warns against hyperfixating on isolated examples due to non-determinism; instead focus on failure patterns across multiple golden-set examples. Advocates investing in online evals and refreshing test sets with production data.

sections.title: Recap: Building Production-Grade Evals
sections.summary: Recaps characteristics of a good eval system: representative of product goals (differing between MVP and production), continuously evolving with online evals and refreshed test sets, curated golden sets, trained scale raters with clear rubrics and templates, and well-chosen launch metrics with early-defined gatekeeping criteria. Q&A addresses human vs. LLM-as-judge usage, noting disagreement rate monitoring and sampling pipelines apply broadly across use cases.

demonstrations: Disclaimer-removal bug: agent was explicitly told disclaimers can never be removed, yet in edge cases it detected a disclaimer ('paid by the community of parks') on a public parks ad and removed it anyway—a failure only caught by inspecting trace logs, not categorical pass rates
limitations: Generative AI outputs are non-deterministic—can succeed once and fail on another attempt
Jumping to scaled raters too early causes big ups and downs during iteration
Agents do not generalize well depending on training data distributions
Categorical pass/fail metrics cannot reveal why an agent failed or succeeded
Hyperfixating on isolated examples rather than patterns leads to unreliable prompt changes in non-deterministic systems

technologies.label: LLM-as-Judge for Agent Evaluation
technologies.summary: LLM-as-Judge is an evaluation technique where an LLM is used as an automated rater to score or assess agent outputs at scale, complementing or replacing human raters. The speakers describe using LLM/auto raters as the system matures beyond intuition-based 'vibing' and human scale raters. They emphasize monitoring agreement and disagreement rates between human and LLM raters to track calibration trends, going beyond pass/fail by examining agent traces, and conducting spot checks on the LLM judge's reasoning to ensure trustworthiness. The technique is presented as a scaling mechanism that enables evaluation volume infeasible with human raters alone, but only trustworthy when properly calibrated against a high-quality human ground truth with broad use-case coverage.
technologies.role: Core evaluation methodology; the speakers describe their LLM-as-judge system for evaluating YouTube Ads agent outputs, including monitoring agreement rates with human raters, examining agent traces beyond pass/fail, and conducting spot checks on the LLM's reasoning to maintain trust.

technologies.label: Critique Agent with Remediation Loop
technologies.summary: The Critique Agent with Remediation Loop is an agent architecture pattern where an independent agent reviews another agent's output and attempts self-correction before final delivery. The speakers recommend adding this as a foundational architectural component before attempting agent-level evaluation. The critique agent serves as a first line of defense, catching errors at generation time and reducing the burden on downstream evaluation. This pattern is positioned alongside the optimization of LLM-friendly tools as a prerequisite to meaningful agent-level evals, ensuring that tool-level and self-correction issues are addressed before measuring end-to-end agent quality.
technologies.role: Foundational architecture recommendation; the speakers advocate adding an independent critique agent with remediation loops for self-correction as a prerequisite before attempting agent-level evaluation, positioning it alongside LLM-friendly tool optimization as agent foundation work.

technologies.label: Agent Trace Inspection
technologies.summary: Agent Trace Inspection is the practice of examining agent execution traces and logs to diagnose failures that are invisible to categorical pass-rate metrics. The speakers demonstrate its value with a concrete disclaimer-removal bug: despite explicit instructions that disclaimers can never be removed, the agent detected a disclaimer ('paid by the community of parks') on a public parks ad and removed it anyway. The trace showed the agent acknowledging the rule yet violating it, a failure mode completely invisible to aggregate pass/fail metrics. The speakers argue that trace inspection is essential for understanding why an agent failed or succeeded, complementing categorical metrics rather than replacing them. External research corroborates this: the GroundEval paper demonstrates that trace-level deterministic evaluation reveals failures that LLM-as-judge misses, with two frontier LLM judges scoring a plausible agent response above 0.85 while the trace showed the agent never retrieved the artifact its answer depended on.
technologies.role: Key diagnostic technique demonstrated with the disclaimer-removal bug example; speakers show that trace inspection reveals failure modes invisible to categorical pass-rate metrics, making it essential for production agent debugging.

technologies.label: Golden Set Construction and Evaluation Methodology
technologies.summary: Golden Set Construction is the practice of building curated collections of test cases (positive and negative) used to evaluate agent behavior, with multiple examples per failure pattern to account for non-deterministic outputs. The speakers recommend starting small with core tasks and negative tests, then expanding the golden set gradually. This is embedded within a broader evolutionary evaluation methodology that progresses from intuition-based 'vibing' to scaled human raters to LLM-as-judge. The methodology encompasses hill climbing through iterative eval-agent co-development (reviewing eval sets, computing precision and recall, adjusting models and tooling), running ablation experiments for causal analysis, understanding regressions to distinguish acceptable trade-offs from critical failures, refreshing test sets with production data, investing in online evals, and defining clear launch gatekeeping criteria with precision/recall thresholds early in development.
technologies.role: Overarching evaluation framework; the speakers describe their complete methodology including golden set construction starting small with core tasks and negative tests, hill climbing through eval-agent co-development with precision/recall and ablations, regression analysis for launch readiness, test set refresh with production data, online evals, and launch gatekeeping criteria.

prerequisites: Familiarity with LLM-based agent architectures and tool-calling patterns
Understanding of basic evaluation metrics including precision, recall, and F1 score
Experience with prompt engineering for LLM applications
Basic knowledge of human rating methodologies and rubric design
Awareness of non-determinism in generative AI model outputs
outcomes: Describe an evolutionary approach to building evals for agents — from intuition-based vibing to scaled human raters to LLM-as-judge — and articulate when each stage is appropriate
Diagnose agent failures through trace inspection rather than relying on categorical pass-rate metrics alone, using the disclaimer-removal bug as a concrete case study
Determine when to use intuition-based versus formal evaluation approaches during different phases of agent development
Apply hill climbing through iterative eval-agent co-development, computing precision and recall on eval sets and running ablation experiments
Distinguish acceptable trade-offs from critical failures by analyzing regression patterns across multiple golden-set examples rather than isolated runs
Design multi-output evaluation rubrics that capture accuracy, brand safety, and expected behavior dimensions with clear rater instructions
Construct golden sets with multiple examples covering the same pattern to account for agent non-determinism and reduce evaluation volatility
Monitor human-LLM judge agreement rates and conduct spot checks on LLM reasoning to maintain evaluation quality at scale
Define launch gatekeeping criteria with appropriate metrics and thresholds for production agent deployment readiness
Plan ongoing evaluation maintenance including online evals, test-set refresh with production data, and golden-set evolution as use cases mature
challengeSeeds: Build a golden set with 10 positive and 5 negative test cases for an agent that processes advertising creatives, ensuring at least 2 examples per failure pattern to account for non-determinism
Implement an LLM-as-judge evaluator and measure its agreement rate against a human-labeled calibration set of 50 examples, targeting at least 75% agreement before deployment
Given an agent trace log containing a hidden guardrail violation, identify the failure point that categorical pass-rate metrics would miss and explain why trace inspection was necessary

Design a launch gatekeeping rubric with precision and recall thresholds for a creative-processing agent, including criteria for classifying regressions as acceptable trade-offs versus critical failures
Create a pattern-based evaluation dashboard that aggregates failure occurrences across multiple golden-set runs and flags recurring patterns rather than reporting isolated individual failures

Build a critique agent with a remediation loop that reviews another agent's output and attempts self-correction before final delivery, then evaluate its impact on overall quality using ablation experiments
